levels.title: Cortex, wiring and modulation: from maps to habits and the appraisal of brain claims

lessons.title: Cortical maps and topographic organisation: what a map claim requires
lessons.explanation: Objective: define a topographic map, a receptive field and a magnification factor, and state what measurements would make a claim that a cortical area 'contains a map' precise. A topographic map means that neighbourhood relations in a receptor sheet are preserved in the cortex: cells that sit next to each other in the retina or on the skin send their signals to neighbouring cortical sites. The open electronic textbook Neuroscience Online states the visual case directly in Section 2, Chapter 15, under 'The Visual Pathway from Retina to Cortex' and 'Retinotopic Organization in the Visual Pathway': a topographic map of the visual fields is laid out in the medial wall of the occipital lobe, and the same chapter works through how damage at different points of that pathway produces characteristic field losses. The somatosensory chapter makes the parallel claim under 'Spatial Information is Topographically Mapped in Sensory Pathways' and locates the body representation in the postcentral gyrus. Three qualifications matter. First, a map is not a photograph: it is distorted, because the density of receptors and the amount of cortex devoted to a body part or visual field differ enormously, which is what a magnification factor quantifies. Second, receptive fields overlap, so a given cortical cell responds to a region of the receptor surface rather than to a point; the smaller the receptive field, the finer the spatial information that cell can carry. Third, map boundaries depend on how you measure them: threshold, resolution and the statistical test all change where the border lands. A map claim, then, is a claim about systematic neighbourhood relations under a stated measurement.
lessons.example: Work the arithmetic of magnification. Suppose a hypothetical measurement finds that the central 2 degrees of visual angle occupy 10 mm of cortex, giving 5 mm per degree, while a location 20 degrees out occupies 5 mm per 10 degrees, giving 0.5 mm per degree. The ratio is 10, so central vision gets ten times as much cortical distance per degree of visual angle. Now suppose the experiment samples the cortex with 1 mm voxels. Near the centre, one voxel spans about 0.2 degrees of visual angle; in the periphery it spans about 2 degrees. The same voxel size therefore resolves neighbourhood relations about ten times more coarsely in the periphery, so an unsmoothed 'map' figure will look crisp in the centre and blurred at the edge for purely geometric reasons. Run the same logic in touch. If a commonly cited textbook two-point discrimination threshold is roughly 2.5 mm at the fingertip and roughly 40 mm on the upper back, the ratio is about 16. That ratio is real and measurable, but it is not automatically explained by cortical magnification: receptor density, receptive field size at each relay, and the number of afferents per unit skin all contribute, and a cortical map claim needs the measurement chain spelled out rather than a single satisfying story.
lessons.question: A study reports that neighbouring stimulus positions activate neighbouring cortical sites and concludes that 'the cortex contains a map of the body'. What would make that claim precise rather than merely evocative?
lessons.answer: Stating the mapped variable, the cortical axes, the stimulus set and the measurement resolution, and showing that neighbourhood relations hold beyond the smoothing and threshold used to draw the figure.
lessons.distractor: Showing that a small spot of cortex responds strongly to the body, since a localised response is the same thing as a map.
lessons.correction: A single activated region is a spot, not a map. A map claim requires an ordering: neighbouring positions on the receptor sheet must produce neighbouring positions in cortex, measured with enough samples to define neighbours. Resolution and threshold decide where borders fall, so they must be reported. The distinction between a spot and a map is the difference between saying where activity is and saying how activity is arranged.

depth.definitions: A topographic map is a systematic neighbourhood-preserving projection from a receptor surface to a neural structure. A receptive field is the region of the receptor surface whose stimulation changes a given cell's firing. The magnification factor is the amount of cortical distance or volume per unit of receptor surface (per degree of visual angle, per millimetre of skin). Retinotopy is the visual case; somatotopy is the body case; tonotopy is the auditory case for frequency rather than space. Population receptive field (pRF) mapping is a model-based method that fits each voxel's preferred position and size rather than reading a border by eye; the Silver and Kastner review discusses measurement approaches in its first box. Prerequisites: transduction and adaptation from lesson 36, receptive fields and centre-surround organisation from lesson 23, and the imaging-inference cautions from lessons 27 and 40.
depth.mechanism: Maps are not installed once and left alone. Development establishes a coarse order through molecular guidance: Neuroscience Online's chapter on synapse formation, survival and elimination, in Section 9.7 'Target Recognition-Topographic Maps', describes how axonal projections come to be ordered, and the chapter's later sections on presynaptic and postsynaptic differentiation describe how contacts mature. Graded chemical cues and activity then refine the order. In adults the map is still measurable but continually variable: the eLife study by Liu and colleagues used 7 T fMRI and behavioural tests to ask how meso-scale topographic maps in somatosensory cortex are organised in younger and older adults, and its framing is that maps can be less sharply differentiated than the textbook picture suggests, with the interesting question being whether organisation relates to behaviour. That is a live question rather than a settled result, so read the paper's Results before repeating any summary of it. The mechanism sentence to carry forward is therefore layered: coarse chemical ordering, activity-dependent refinement, and a measurable adult organisation whose sharpness depends on age, attention, and the method used to probe it.
depth.secondExample: Contrast a retinotopic measurement with a somatotopic one. Retinotopic mapping can use a travelling-wave stimulus that sweeps through many positions in a few minutes, giving hundreds of samples and a phase value per voxel, which is why visual maps are drawn with fine borders. Somatotopic mapping usually stimulates a small number of discrete sites, so the map is constructed from fewer, larger samples and its borders are correspondingly coarser. Now contrast either of those with a claim that 'the brain area for the fingers is here': that is a localisation claim about a body part, not a map claim about ordering, and it can be true while the ordering itself is only weakly measured. Keeping these three claims apart — ordering, location, and responsivity — prevents a response blob from being redescribed as a map.
depth.mistake: The common misconception is that a map equals localisation of psychological function, so that finding a region responsive to faces or to nouns is treated as finding the brain's face area or noun area. Diagnostic correction: ask what the map's axes are made of and what stimulus property defines them. A topographic map is defined by an ordering along a sensory surface, not by a cognitive category. A second version of the mistake is treating the drawn border as a natural kind; borders move with smoothing kernel, threshold and sample size, which is why the same cortex appears differently mapped across papers.
depth.application: Task: find one published cortical map figure and write a four-line audit. Line 1: the mapped variable and its axis units. Line 2: the stimulus set and how many distinct positions were sampled. Line 3: the spatial resolution of the measurement and the smoothing or threshold used. Line 4: one sentence on what would falsify the ordering. Self-review rubric: award a point for each line that states a number rather than an adjective; deduct a point if the audit describes a region's function rather than its ordering; deduct a point if the audit cannot say what would count as a disagreement between two studies of the same area.
depth.summary: A cortical map is a measurement-dependent regularity: neighbourhood relations preserved under a stated stimulus set and resolution, embedded in a distorted sheet with overlapping receptive fields. Development supplies coarse order through molecular guidance, experience refines it, and adult organisation remains variable. Transfer the audit habit to any claim that a region 'maps' something: ask for the axes, the samples and the threshold before accepting the picture.

lessons.title: How experience wires circuits: pruning, critical periods, and two kinds of plasticity
lessons.explanation: Objective: explain how developing circuits are initially over-produced and then refined, what makes a critical period open and close, and why the distinction between experience-expectant and experience-dependent plasticity is useful but not absolute. The wiring problem is not building connections from nothing; it is producing many more connections than the adult brain keeps and then selecting among them. Neuroscience Online's chapter on synapse formation, survival and elimination covers the front end of this process: axon pathfinding, growth cones, guidepost cells, fasciculation and guidance forces, then target recognition and topographic maps (Section 9.7), and finally the molecular mechanisms of presynaptic and postsynaptic differentiation. Selection comes after that: contacts that are active and correlated tend to persist, while others are withdrawn, so the adult pattern reflects both an initial rule-governed layout and subsequent activity-driven editing. Two vocabularies are used for the experience side. Experience-expectant plasticity refers to refinement that depends on information the species can expect to be present, such as patterned light reaching the retina, and it concentrates in early sensitive windows. Experience-dependent plasticity refers to changes driven by an individual's particular learning history and continues throughout life. The distinction is a working framework rather than a boundary in the tissue: recent reviews re-examine the criteria that define a critical period, and one of them argues explicitly that critical periods for network composition should be distinguished from the classical sensory ones. Two mechanisms explain the closing side: maturation of inhibitory circuitry gates onset, and structural braking factors such as perineuronal nets and myelination limit further reorganisation. The practical consequence is asymmetry: a system inside a sensitive window may be changed by experience that would do little afterwards, and that cuts both ways, because deprivation and enrichment both exert larger effects there.
lessons.example: Make the timing arithmetic explicit. Suppose the sensitive period for one visual function is usually described as running from birth to about age 8. If a child has a period of abnormal input from age 2 to age 6, that covers 4 of the 8 years, or half the window, and the portion remaining afterwards is 2 years, or a quarter of the window. Now compare an intervention starting at age 3 with one starting at age 5 under a model in which plasticity declines roughly exponentially with a time constant of 2 years. A simple half-life calculation gives e raised to minus 0.5, about 0.61, of the initial plasticity remaining at 1 year, and e raised to minus 1, about 0.37, at 2 years; moving the start from 3 to 5 years therefore leaves the system with roughly 37 per cent rather than 61 per cent of the early capacity. These are illustrative numbers for arithmetic practice, not measured constants, and real estimates vary by function and by measure. Run the same logic on synapse counts. If a hypothetical cortical region carries 12,000 synapses per neuron at age 2 and 7,000 in adulthood, the reduction is 5,000, or about 42 per cent. If a study reports a 15 per cent difference in synapse density between two groups at age 20, that difference is a fraction of the earlier elimination: comparing 15 with 42 shows that a large part of the developmental change is over before the age at which most adult studies sample, which is one reason cross-sectional adult studies struggle to recover developmental processes.
lessons.question: A review reports that critical period onset depends on the maturation of inhibitory circuitry while closure depends on perineuronal nets and myelination. Why does splitting onset from closure matter for the interpretation of an intervention study?
lessons.answer: Because a window has two independently controlled edges, so an intervention's effect depends both on whether inhibition has matured enough for plasticity to be gated open and on how much structural braking has already accumulated.
lessons.distractor: Because onset mechanisms mean the window can be reopened at any time, so structural braking is only a descriptive label for something already reversible.
lessons.correction: The two edges behave differently: opening is a permissive gating event, while closure involves accumulating structural constraints, so reopening a closed window is a different experimental problem from extending an open one. A study that manipulates experience without stating where it sits inside the window cannot be compared cleanly with one at a different age, because the same manipulation can fall on either side of the onset gate or run into the braking mechanisms.

depth.definitions: A critical period is a developmental window during which an experience has a large and often lasting effect that the same experience produces weakly or not at all outside the window. A sensitive period is the weaker claim: effects are larger earlier, without a sharp boundary. Synapse elimination or pruning is the withdrawal of some contacts as others are stabilised. Perineuronal nets are extracellular matrix structures that form around certain neurons, especially fast-spiking inhibitory cells, and constrain structural change. Myelination is the wrapping of axons by oligodendrocytes, which changes conduction and also limits sprouting. Prerequisites: synaptic plasticity from lessons 25 and 33, and the transduction and receptive field material from lesson 36.
depth.mechanism: The reviewed sequence runs as follows. Guidance molecules and activity produce a roughly ordered but over-connected system; inhibition matures, and once inhibition can shape the timing of activity, the system becomes sensitive to the statistics of its input; correlated activity then reinforces some contacts and removes others; finally, structural braking factors accumulate and shrink the range of change. Begum and Sng's review of experience-dependent maturation in cortical GABAergic inhibition places inhibitory circuit development at the centre of critical period onset and works through signalling molecules and BDNF at the transcription and protein level, plus epigenetic regulation. Larsen and Luna organise the facilitating factors (inhibition, excitation, BDNF, experience itself) and the braking factors (perineuronal nets, myelination) into a two-sided account, and then ask whether adolescence is a critical period for association cortex; their answer is that the early sensory literature supplies the criteria but the adolescent case remains an active research question. Dehorter and Del Pino go further and argue that the criteria defining critical periods need re-examination, including the distinction between classical sensory periods and periods that shape network composition, and they discuss attempts to model human critical periods in vitro.
depth.secondExample: Contrast two deprivations with different outcomes. In early monocular deprivation, one eye's patterned input is removed during a sensitive window, and cortical representations shift toward the non-deprived eye in the classic animal literature; the deprivation is effective because it removes expected input inside the window. In adult skill learning, a musician acquiring fine timing or a reader acquiring a writing system does not depend on the same expected input and does not close behind a window in the same way; here the change is experience-dependent, individually variable, and slower. The two cases share molecules and mechanisms but differ in what would count as deprivation: removing expected input is catastrophic early, while failing to practise a skill only means not acquiring that skill. Conflating them produces the false claim that adults cannot learn, which the same literature does not support.
depth.mistake: The frequent mistake is to read critical periods as absolute and global: the brain is 'finished' at some age and nothing changes after. Diagnostic correction: ask which function, which measure, and which window. Windows differ in timing and duration across systems, some are better described as sensitive than critical, and adult plasticity clearly exists. A second mistake is to treat pruning as loss: the reduction in synapse number accompanies refinement of the remaining contacts, so counting contacts without measuring their organisation or function will mislead. A third is to read a group average as an individual timeline; developmental timing varies widely between people.
depth.application: Task: design a one-page protocol for a hypothetical study of whether a training programme has a larger effect at one age than another, using established critical period reasoning. Include: the function to be trained and the measure used; at least three age bands with stated sample sizes; the predicted direction under a critical period account and under a sensitive period account, which differ in whether the effect should drop sharply or gradually; one braking-factor measure if available in your setting; and a statement of what result would count against the critical period reading. Self-review rubric: a point for a measurable outcome; a point for age bands that can distinguish a sharp boundary from a gradient; a point for specifying a falsifying pattern; a point deducted for any sentence that asserts a hidden mechanism that the design cannot touch.
depth.summary: Developing cortex over-produces contacts and then selects among them using activity, with inhibition gating when selection can occur and structural braking factors limiting it later. Experience-expectant refinement inside windows and experience-dependent learning throughout life are best treated as a continuum of constraints rather than two worlds. Transfer: whenever a claim uses 'critical period', ask for the function, the measure, the window's two edges, and whether the design could distinguish a sharp boundary from a gradual decline.

lessons.title: Dopamine: prediction error, effort, and why 'the pleasure molecule' is a misreading
lessons.explanation: Objective: state what midbrain dopamine neurons do in the best-supported accounts of learning and motivation, and dismantle three popular misreadings. The dopamine system is anatomically distributed, not one wire: Neuroscience Online's chapter on biogenic amines distinguishes the anatomy of the catecholamines and maps dopamine pathways separately from norepinephrine pathways (Sections 12.2, 12.4 and 12.5), and the same textbook's basal ganglia chapter states that dopaminergic neurons signal unexpected reward or the unexpected absence of reward. That sentence is where the modern account starts. In the reward prediction error account that Glimcher reviews, dopamine neurons carry a teaching signal: firing rises above baseline when an outcome is better than predicted, stays near baseline when the outcome matches the prediction, and dips below baseline when an expected outcome fails to arrive. This signal is what makes learning possible, because it tells the system how wrong its prediction was, not how pleasant the outcome felt. Three corrections follow. First, 'dopamine is pleasure' is wrong in the strong form: Berridge's incentive salience account separates 'wanting' from 'liking' and argues that dopamine contributes to the motivational pull of cues rather than to the hedonic experience itself. Second, 'dopamine is the reward system' is an over-generalisation: Salamone and Correa review evidence that mesolimbic dopamine is important for behavioural activation and for overcoming response costs, and that fundamental motivational and hedonic responses survive interference with it. Third, 'one molecule, one feeling' fails because of heterogeneity: Lerner and colleagues note that dopamine neurons differ in molecular profile and connectivity, that some substantia nigra neurons may not encode prediction error, and that whether the movement, motivation and planning functions can be reconciled with prediction error theory is an open question. None of this licenses a self-directed chemical intervention; the material is educational and does not diagnose or treat anything.
lessons.example: Compute a prediction error by hand. Use the standard temporal difference form, error equals the reward received plus gamma times the value of the next state minus the value of the current state, with gamma set to 0.9 for illustration. Before learning, if a cue is followed by a reward of 1 on every trial and the value of the cue is initially estimated at 0.2, the error on the first rewarded trial is 1 plus 0.9 times 0 minus 0.2, which is 0.8, a strong positive signal. Repeated training raises the cue's estimate toward the actual outcome; once the estimate reaches about 1.0, the error at reward time falls to 1 minus 1.0, which is 0. Now remove the reward while keeping the cue: the error becomes 0 minus 1.0, which is minus 1.0, a strong negative signal, and the estimate will fall on subsequent trials. Do the same exercise with magnitudes. If the expected reward is 10 units and the delivery is 14, the error is plus 4, or 40 per cent above expectation; if delivery is 6, the error is minus 4, or 40 per cent below. The numbers teach the design lesson: a dopamine response that has moved earlier in time, from the reward to the cue that predicts it, is evidence about prediction, not about pleasure, and it can only be interpreted against a stated expected value.
lessons.question: Blocking an expected reward produces a below-baseline dopamine response. Which reading of that result is defensible?
lessons.answer: The response reflects the negative prediction error created when an expected outcome fails to occur, so it tracks the mismatch between outcome and prediction rather than the absence of anything pleasant.
lessons.distractor: The dip proves that the outcome was unpleasant, since a below-baseline signal must encode negative hedonic value.
lessons.correction: The dip is defined relative to the prediction, not relative to a hedonic scale. An omitted reward that was never expected produces little or no dip, while an omitted reward that was reliably predicted produces a large one, which is exactly the behaviour of a prediction error and not of a pleasure signal. Reading hedonic valence into the sign of the signal confuses the quantity a system computes with the feeling a person reports.

depth.definitions: A reward prediction error is the difference between an obtained outcome and its predicted value. Phasic signalling is a brief burst or dip lasting on the order of a few hundred milliseconds, contrasted with tonic activity spread over much longer periods. Incentive salience is the attribution of motivational pull to a cue, described by Berridge as distinct from hedonic impact or 'liking'. Effort-related choice describes behaviour in which an organism chooses between options differing in response cost, a paradigm used by Salamone and Correa. Reinforcement learning is the computational framework in which an agent updates value estimates using prediction errors. Prerequisites: synaptic plasticity from lessons 25 and 33, and the necessity, sufficiency and reverse inference tools from lessons 28 and 29.
depth.mechanism: The mechanism has three layers. At the cellular level, dopamine neurons receive converging inputs that let them compare an outcome with a prediction, and their firing rate encodes the comparison rather than the outcome alone. At the circuit level, dopamine release modulates plasticity in targets such as dorsal and ventral striatum and frontal cortex, so the teaching signal changes how likely actions are to be repeated. At the behavioural level, the consequences include cue-triggered approach, behavioural activation and effort allocation. The layer where the accounts diverge is the last one: prediction error is a good fit for learning, less settled for movement and planning, and the effort account reviewed by Salamone and Correa points to response cost sensitivity as the signature effect of interfering with mesolimbic dopamine. Lerner and colleagues make the divergence explicit rather than hiding it, noting that dopamine neurons are molecularly heterogeneous, that they release more than dopamine, and that whether a single theory can cover all their functions is unclear. The popular 'pleasure molecule' and 'detox' framing sits outside all three layers.
depth.secondExample: Contrast behavioural activation with cue-triggered wanting. In the effort-choice paradigm, animals choose between a preferred outcome that requires work and a less preferred outcome that requires little; interfering with mesolimbic dopamine shifts choice toward the low-cost option while the animals still consume and respond to the preferred outcome when it is free, which is what supports reading dopamine as central to overcoming response cost rather than to the value of the outcome. In the incentive salience paradigm, a cue paired with a reward acquires motivational pull, so a rat will work for the cue itself, and that pull can be dissociated experimentally from the hedonic reaction to the outcome. These two findings are not competitors: one concerns the price of action, the other the pull of a cue. The misreading arises when both are collapsed into 'dopamine equals reward equals pleasure'.
depth.mistake: The dominant popular mistake is the chemical-imbalance style claim that a person's motivation problem is a dopamine deficit and can be fixed by abstaining from pleasure. Diagnostic correction: popularity of a phrase is not evidence, and the strongest form of the claim fails on its own terms, because the brain synthesises dopamine continuously and because tonic depletion produces severe movement disorder rather than selective loss of enjoyment. A second mistake is arguing from a single neurotransmitter to a whole behaviour: naming a molecule is a label, not an explanation, and the explanatory content lies in the circuit, the prediction model and the behavioural paradigm. A third is quote-mining: prediction error theory is often cited to support claims about phone use and productivity that the reviewed work does not address.
depth.application: Task: write a 150-word correction of a popular claim that 'cheap dopamine from scrolling raises your baseline and makes real work feel unrewarding'. Required elements: a clear statement of what the claim asserts; one specific way the prediction error account bears on it; one specific finding from the effort or incentive salience literature that the claim ignores; and a plainly labelled sentence separating the behavioural advice the claim offers from the neurological explanation it attaches to it. Self-review rubric: a point for stating the claim in a form that could be tested; a point for citing a mechanism with its source; a point for distinguishing advice from explanation; a point deducted for any sentence that asserts a measured effect size without a source.
depth.summary: Dopamine neurons carry a prediction error signal that is well supported for learning, a cue-related motivational signal in the incentive salience account, and an effort and activation role in the behavioural economics literature; the unification of these roles remains unresolved. The transferable habit is to refuse the move from one molecule to one feeling, and to ask every time: what was predicted, what was delivered, what was the cost of the action, and which dopamine cells were recorded?

visual.title: Prediction error against the popular picture: five labelled comparisons
visual.description: A comparison diagram placing the measured dopamine signal beside the popular claims about it, with worked numbers for expected and obtained outcomes.

lessons.title: Stress physiology and its cumulative effects on brain and body
lessons.explanation: Objective: trace the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis, distinguish fast neural from slow hormonal arms of the response, and explain why the dose, timing and duration of a stressor determine whether the effect is adaptive or damaging. Stress physiology is a control system, not a chemical mood. Neuroscience Online's chapter on hypothalamic control of pituitary hormones lays out the anterior pituitary and its feedback loops, with a dedicated section on stress, and shows that secretion is governed by feedback rather than by open-loop release: hypothalamic releasing factors drive pituitary hormones, which drive target gland output, which feeds back on the brain. For the stress response specifically, the paraventricular nucleus releases corticotropin-releasing factor, the anterior pituitary releases adrenocorticotropic hormone, and the adrenal cortex secretes cortisol. Running alongside that slow hormonal arm is a fast neural arm: sympathetic outflow and catecholamine release change heart rate, blood pressure and availability of glucose within seconds. The two arms have different clocks, which is why 'stress' is not a single state. Effects on the brain depend on three variables. Dose: glucocorticoid effects on plasticity and memory commonly follow an inverted-U, with intermediate levels enhancing and very low or very high levels impairing. Timing: a growing literature reports facilitation of consolidation and impairment of retrieval, meaning the same hormone does opposite things depending on the memory phase it accompanies. Duration: repeated or sustained activation is where cumulative costs appear, which is what the allostatic load vocabulary describes. Eachus and Ryu review glucocorticoid signalling from adaptive developmental plasticity through to allostatic overload, and their review states plainly that the tipping point at which adaptive plasticity becomes overload is not well defined, and that effects are dose and context dependent; Daskalakis, Meijer and de Kloet add that the two receptor types, mineralocorticoid and glucocorticoid, act in a cell-type-specific manner, so a single whole-brain statement about 'cortisol' is too coarse. This is education about physiology, not diagnosis or treatment.
lessons.example: Build the arithmetic of a feedback loop. Suppose a hypothetical assay reports a morning cortisol concentration of 300 nanomoles per litre and a peak after a laboratory stressor of 700. The peak is 400 above baseline, about 133 per cent higher, and the return toward baseline over the following hour is the measurable part of the negative feedback loop. Now add the circadian rhythm: if the amplitude of the daily oscillation is roughly 60 per cent of the morning value, then the same absolute concentration means different things at 8 a.m. and at 8 p.m., so a study that samples once at an unstated time cannot support a claim about responsivity. Next, the inverted-U: if performance is indexed from 0 to 100 and the fitted curve peaks at a cortisol value of about 400 with a score of 80, while values of 200 and 700 give about 50 and 30, then a linear summary of the same data would have the wrong sign for half the range. Finally, duration. If a stressor increases cortisol by 50 per cent for two hours, that is 100 per cent-hours of excess exposure; the same 50 per cent sustained for eight hours a day gives 400 per cent-hours, four times the exposure with identical peak amplitude. Reporting only the peak hides the quantity most relevant to cumulative effects, which is why reviews of allostatic load count exposures and repeated measures alongside magnitudes.
lessons.question: A study finds that an acute stressor before a test improves performance, and concludes that stress improves memory. Which additional facts must be established before that conclusion is warranted?
lessons.answer: Where on the dose curve the stressor fell, at which memory phase it occurred, and whether the same dose impairs retrieval or, at higher or repeated doses, reverses the effect.
lessons.distractor: Nothing further is needed, because an improvement after a stressor demonstrates that the stress response is beneficial within its physiological range.
lessons.correction: An improvement at one dose and one time point is a point on a curve, and glucocorticoid effects depend on dose, timing and duration. The same manipulation can help consolidation and harm retrieval, and higher or sustained elevations are associated with impairment. Without the dose, the timing and a repeat measure, the result cannot be generalised to stress as a category.

depth.definitions: The hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis is the hormonal chain from paraventricular nucleus to anterior pituitary to adrenal cortex. Cortisol is the main human glucocorticoid. Mineralocorticoid receptors bind glucocorticoids with high affinity and are substantially occupied at low concentrations; glucocorticoid receptors have lower affinity and are recruited more as concentrations rise, which is the basis for a two-receptor, context-sensitive account of signalling. Allostasis is the maintenance of stability through change; allostatic load or overload refers to the cumulative cost of repeated or sustained adjustment. Consolidation is the post-acquisition process that stabilises a memory; retrieval is the later recovery of that memory. Prerequisites: autonomic reflex loops and set-point versus defended range from lesson 38, and the consolidation account from lesson 34.
depth.mechanism: The axis runs as a feedback controller. A challenge is detected and appraised, hypothalamic releasing factor rises, pituitary secretion follows, adrenal output follows, and rising glucocorticoid concentration feeds back on hypothalamus, pituitary and hippocampus to restrain further release; the fast sympathetic arm supplies immediate changes in cardiovascular and metabolic state. The signaling itself is more than one switch: Daskalakis and colleagues describe mineralocorticoid and glucocorticoid receptors working alone and in combination in a cell-type-specific way, which explains how one hormone can stabilise a system at low concentrations and, at sustained high concentrations, contribute to altered excitability, altered structural markers and metabolic cost. Where the literature becomes contested is the transition. Eachus and Ryu title a subsection 'Where is the tipping point?' and answer that it is not sharply defined, then discuss the energetic cost of allostasis and dose- and context-dependent effects. That means the honest formulation is graded: sustained activation is associated with costs, the thresholds are individual and context-dependent, and the same physiology supports adaptation when it is brief and repeated adaptation when it is not.
depth.secondExample: Contrast an exam week with a chronic caregiving situation as a purely descriptive exercise. In the exam case the challenge is bounded, the peak is high and the baseline is mostly restored, so the measurable signature is a large transient: recovery time is the interesting variable. In sustained caregiving the peaks may be lower but the number of hours per day above baseline is large, so the signature is a raised trough with blunted daily rhythm, and the cumulative exposure is much greater even if no single measurement looks dramatic. The lesson's arithmetic is that exposure is amplitude multiplied by duration, so a lower-amplitude, long-duration profile can exceed a high-amplitude short one. The contradiction to avoid is treating them as the same phenomenon because both are called stress; the interpretation depends on the temporal profile, and the reviewed sources are explicit that context changes the direction of effects.
depth.mistake: The most common misconception is that cortisol is simply 'the stress hormone' and that lower is better. Diagnostic correction: glucocorticoids are necessary for normal function, low and intermediate concentrations support plasticity and consolidation, and the defect state depends on the receptor population and the tissue examined, not on a global direction. A second mistake is to treat a single saliva or blood sample as a measure of a person's stress load; time of day, eating, sleep and recent activity all move the value, and the reviews cited here build their accounts on repeated measures and challenge protocols. A third is to convert physiology into instruction, for example by adopting supplements or extreme routines to 'lower cortisol'. Nothing in this material supports self-directed intervention, and the honest use of it is interpretive.
depth.application: Task: given a hypothetical report that a group of students showed higher cortisol and worse recall in a two-week exam period, write a five-sentence evaluation. Required content: whether the design can separate duration from peak; what retrieval-versus-consolidation confound may be present; one measurement limitation; one alternative explanation that does not require the stress axis at all, such as sleep restriction or practice differences; and one sentence on what would raise confidence, such as repeated sampling with recovery measures and a control period. Self-review rubric: a point for correctly distinguishing amplitude from duration; a point for naming the memory phase; a point for a non-hormonal alternative; a point deducted for any recommendation to change a person's physiology, and a point deducted for treating a group difference as an individual prediction.
depth.summary: The stress response is a two-arm feedback system with a fast neural limb and a slow glucocorticoid limb signalled through two receptors with different affinities. Effects on brain function depend on dose, timing and duration, with inverted-U dose relations and opposite effects during consolidation and retrieval, while cumulative cost is best described as graded allostatic load whose tipping point the reviewed literature does not claim to have fixed. Transfer: before generalising any stress result, ask for the profile over time, the memory phase, and the receptor and tissue context.

lessons.title: Sleep as a controlled system: two processes, arousal circuits, and what sleep changes
lessons.explanation: Objective: describe the two-process model of sleep regulation, name the circuits that stabilise waking and sleep, and state which sleep claims the sources support and which remain contested. Sleep is not the absence of waking activity; it is a regulated state produced by the interaction of a homeostatic process and a circadian process. The two-process model, whose origins and current status Borbely himself reviews in the Journal of Sleep Research, proposes a sleep-wake-dependent process, conventionally called Process S, which accumulates during wakefulness and discharges during sleep, interacting with a circadian process, Process C, generated by the internal clock. Slow-wave activity in the electroencephalogram during non-rapid-eye-movement sleep is the classical marker used for Process S. Two companion papers in this lesson's readings take opposite tones on how settled this is. Borbely's retrospective explains how the model was built from animal experiments and human data and how it has been tested. Dijk's 2026 perspective assembles human data collected across roughly forty years that are at odds with parts of the model as originally stated: the assumption about when circadian drive to wakefulness peaks in humans is described as incorrect, slow-wave activity is questioned as a clean biomarker of recovery, and the two processes are argued to interact continuously rather than adding simply. A well-informed learner therefore keeps the two-process framework as the organising model while refusing to treat its parameters as laws. The circuits that stabilise state are also worth naming: wake-promoting neurons in the brainstem and basal forebrain, sleep-promoting neurons in the preoptic area, and orexin/hypocretin neurons in the lateral hypothalamus, whose loss produces narcolepsy type 1 with its instability of state boundaries. That is a claim about state control, not about the function of sleep, which is a separate and harder question.
lessons.example: Run the model's arithmetic as an illustration. Suppose sleep pressure accumulates during wakefulness toward an asymptote with an 18-hour time constant. After 16 hours awake the value is one minus e raised to minus 16 divided by 18, which is one minus e raised to minus 0.889, about 0.589, so pressure is roughly 59 per cent of the way to asymptote. After 8 hours asleep with a 4-hour decay constant, pressure falls to e raised to minus 2, about 0.135, of its starting value, so it is mostly discharged rather than fully reset, which is a testable prediction: a shorter night should leave measurable residual pressure. Now do the cycle arithmetic that a lab report needs. An eight-hour night is 480 minutes; at roughly 90 minutes per cycle that is about 5.3 cycles, so a statement about events in the fifth cycle concerns the final third of the night. If slow-wave activity is concentrated early, the same 480 minutes contains much more of it in the first 160 minutes than in the last 160, so a protocol that samples only the second half will systematically underestimate slow-wave-dependent effects. Finally, resolve timing so the method matches the claim: a 14 Hz spindle has a period of about 71 milliseconds while a 0.8 Hz slow oscillation has a period of 1250 milliseconds, a ratio of about 18, so a recording or analysis step that cannot resolve 71 milliseconds cannot support a claim about spindles even if it captures slow oscillations adequately. These constants are chosen for arithmetic practice; the sources should be consulted for the values actually fitted to data.
lessons.question: A review reports that some human data are at odds with slow-wave activity as a biomarker of sleep homeostasis. What is the correct response to that disagreement?
lessons.answer: Keep the model as an organising framework while treating slow-wave activity as a contested marker, and cite the disagreement rather than presenting homeostasis as established measurement.
lessons.distractor: Discard the two-process model, because a biomarker that is questioned invalidates the framework that used it.
lessons.correction: A model and its proxy measure have different evidentiary status. The interaction of a homeostatic and a circadian process survives as a framework even if one proxy is imperfect, and the way to handle the dispute is to state both the model's predictions and the specific departures documented in human data. The error is to collapse 'this marker does not behave as predicted in some conditions' into 'sleep regulation is not homeostatic', or alternatively to ignore the departures because the framework is influential.

depth.definitions: Process S is the homeostatic component, accumulating during wake and discharging during sleep; Process C is the circadian component generated by the suprachiasmatic nucleus and entrained by light. Slow-wave activity is electroencephalographic power in the slow-wave band during non-rapid-eye-movement sleep, used as a proxy for Process S. Sleep propensity is the tendency to fall asleep at a given moment, modelled as a combination of the two processes. A flip-flop or bistable switch is a circuit arrangement in which mutually inhibitory populations make intermediate states unstable, which is one account of why sleep and waking are discrete. Orexin, also called hypocretin, is a lateral hypothalamic neuropeptide that excites wake-promoting nuclei. Narcolepsy type 1 is the disorder associated with loss of orexin-producing neurons, including cataplexy. Prerequisites: the consolidation material in lesson 35 and the oscillation and recording-resolution logic in lesson 39.
depth.mechanism: The framework's mechanism is an interaction between a saturating accumulator and a self-sustaining oscillator: sleep pressure rises across the day, the circadian system opens and closes periods in which sleep is permissible, and the two together set when sleep is initiated and how intense it is. The neurobiological substrate of the accumulator is not fully settled; adenosine accumulation is a widely discussed candidate. The stabilising circuits are better characterised: orexin neurons in the lateral hypothalamus are tonically active during wakefulness and excite noradrenergic, histaminergic and cholinergic arousal systems, which is why their loss produces not just sleepiness but an instability of state boundaries, with rapid transitions into rapid-eye-movement sleep and with muscle tone lost during waking in cataplexy. Inutsuka and Yamanaka review the orexin system in exactly these terms, and Schone and Burdakov argue that stability of waking cannot be explained by redundancy alone because loss of this single system breaks it. Notice the asymmetry in the sources: state control is well supported by converging animal and human evidence, whereas the functional question, what sleep is for, remains contested and is discussed in lesson 35 rather than settled here.
depth.secondExample: Contrast two claims that are often made in the same paragraph. Claim one: sleep is required for the consolidation of some memories, supported by cueing and by the electrophysiological work discussed in lesson 35, with the caveat that the human measurements rely on proxies. Claim two: sleep clears metabolic waste from the brain, so poor sleep damages the brain. The register differs: one is an active research area with specific experimental paradigms and identifiable competing hypotheses, while the other is frequently stated in general-audience writing with a mechanistic confidence that the primary literature does not supply, and the human significance of the candidate clearance mechanisms is debated. The lesson's discipline is to ask, for each claim, what was measured, in which species, by what method, and with what effect size, and then to place it on a scale from measured to hypothesised rather than treating all sleep claims as equally established.
depth.mistake: The reliable mistake is to treat the two-process model as a completed physiological mechanism rather than a compact model that predicts behaviour from two variables. Diagnostic correction: ask which prediction was tested and which proxy measured each process. A second mistake is to attribute functions to the whole state of sleep on the basis of a correlational difference between sleepers and non-sleepers, where sleep loss also changes mood, attention and effort. A third is to read a sleep-stage difference in a group as a personal diagnosis, which the educational framing here rules out, and a fourth is to extrapolate animal mechanistic findings to human practice, for example by adopting a supplement or a schedule based on an animal result.
depth.application: Task: take a popular claim that a specific sleep intervention improves learning, and write a 120-word appraisal with the following elements: the claim in one sentence; which process, S or C, the intervention is said to target; the measurement that would distinguish a change in sleep timing from a change in sleep intensity; one plausible confound such as total sleep time or testing time of day; and one sentence stating what result would weaken the claim. Self-review rubric: a point for naming the process targeted; a point for a measurement that separates timing from intensity; a point for identifying a confound that could produce the same result without the claimed mechanism; a point deducted for asserting a function of sleep without evidence, and a point deducted for any statement that prescribes a schedule or supplement.
depth.summary: Sleep is regulated by the interaction of a homeostatic accumulator and a circadian oscillator, stabilised by specific arousal and sleep-promoting circuits including the orexin system, and measured through proxies such as slow-wave activity whose behaviour is itself contested. Transfer: distinguish regulation claims from function claims, match the measurement to the timescale in question, and report the disputes in the sources instead of presenting a tidy mechanism.

questions.prompt: A laboratory reports that the cortical territory devoted to the hand is much larger than that devoted to the back, and concludes that the cortex therefore contains a map of the body surface. Which further result is required before the word map is doing any work?
questions.answer: Evidence that neighbouring body sites project to neighbouring cortical sites, with the sampling resolution and threshold stated.
questions.distractor: Evidence that the hand representation contains more neurons than the back representation, since map size is a count of cells.
questions.correction: Territory size is a magnification claim; ordering is the map claim, and a large representation could exist with scrambled internal order. The claim needs neighbourhood relations measured at a stated resolution, because borders move with threshold and smoothing. Neuron counting addresses a different question and is not what makes a projection topographic.

questions.prompt: An intervention is given at age 5 and at age 14. The younger group improves more, and the authors conclude that the intervention works only before age 6. What would make the stronger wording defensible?
questions.answer: Matched dose, matched measurement and demonstrated absence of an effect later, which is what separates a critical period from a gradual sensitive period decline.
questions.distractor: Nothing further, since a difference in effect size between two ages establishes that the window has closed.
questions.correction: A larger effect earlier is compatible with a gradient of sensitivity rather than a closed window, and unmatched dose, task or measurement could produce the difference on their own. The vocabulary distinction matters because the two readings make different predictions about interventions at an intermediate age, and the intermediate prediction is testable.

questions.prompt: When dopamine transmission is interfered with, animals press less for a preferred food but still consume it readily when it is freely available. Which reading fits this pattern?
questions.answer: A role in the behavioural activation and effort required to obtain an outcome, not in the value of the outcome itself.
questions.distractor: A role in hedonic pleasure, since the reduction in pressing shows that the food stopped being enjoyable.
questions.correction: If the outcome had lost its value, consumption would fall too; preserved consumption with reduced work indicates that the cost of action is what changed. This pattern is what the effort-related literature reports, and it is distinct from both the prediction error role in learning and the incentive salience role in the pull of predictive cues.

questions.prompt: Students tested during examination week show higher cortisol and worse memory test performance than during a control week. What is the minimum additional information needed before calling this an effect of stress hormones on memory?
questions.answer: Whether testing coincided with retrieval or consolidation, the duration and amplitude profile of the cortisol elevation, and whether sleep or practice changed in parallel.
questions.distractor: Nothing, provided the cortisol difference is statistically significant and the sample is large.
questions.correction: Glucocorticoid effects depend on dose, timing and duration, and the reported association could equally reflect short sleep, changed practice or testing conditions. A single comparison cannot separate retrieval effects from consolidation effects, and it cannot distinguish an exposure total from a peak. Group-level association also does not license a prediction about any individual student.

questions.prompt: A sleep protocol records only the last four hours of an eight-hour night and reports that slow-wave measures do not track overnight learning. What is the main design problem?
questions.answer: Slow-wave activity is concentrated in the first part of the night, so the sampled window substantially misses the measure the hypothesis concerns.
questions.distractor: Slow-wave activity is confined to the first hour, so no recording after the first hour can detect it at all.
questions.correction: Concentration is graded, not all-or-none: the first third of a 480-minute night contains much more slow-wave activity than the last third, which biases the estimate strongly even though some activity persists. The correct fix is to record the whole night or to state the window as a limitation. The over-statement in the distractor errs in the opposite direction by making the measure impossible after the first hour.

units.title: Networks, habits and the appraisal of evidence

lessons.title: Language and its lateralisation: dissociations, networks, and the limits of left-right claims
lessons.explanation: Objective: use the classic aphasia evidence correctly, describe the modern network and dual-stream accounts that replaced the simple localisation picture, and state what lateralisation does and does not license. The classical story is that damage to the inferior left frontal region produces effortful, telegraphic speech with relatively preserved comprehension, while damage to the posterior superior temporal region produces fluent but empty speech with impaired comprehension; Neuroscience Online's chapter on higher cortical functions devotes sections to language disorders including Broca, Wernicke, conduction, transcortical and global patterns, and a separate section to right-hemisphere involvement in prosody. Those dissociations remain instructional because they show that separable components of language can break independently. What has changed is the interpretation. Dronkers, Ivanova and Baldo review two centuries of this research and describe how the field moved from lesion-symptom mapping of single regions to network approaches, and how imaging methods including voxel-based mapping, diffusion imaging and functional imaging changed the questions asked. Gupta and Srivastava describe the shift from the Wernicke-Lichtheim model to a dual-stream account, in which a dorsal stream supports mapping from sound to articulation and a ventral stream supports sound to meaning, with subcortical structures including the thalamus contributing. Two cautions follow. First, the classic syndrome names are convenient but imperfect: the lesions that produce the clinical picture are usually larger than the regions named after them, and similar syndromes can arise from different damage, which weakens any claim that a small named area is the module for that function. Second, lateralisation is a graded, population-level statement about relative involvement; it is not a statement that one hemisphere does language and the other does something else, since the right hemisphere's contribution to prosody and other aspects is well documented.
lessons.example: Work a lateralisation arithmetic illustration. Suppose a hypothetical series classifies 62 right-handed participants and finds left-dominant language activation in 60 of them; that is 96.8 per cent, and the 2 remaining are right-dominant or bilateral. For 20 left-handed participants, if 13 show left dominance, the proportion is 65 per cent, and the remaining 7 divide between right dominance and bilateral patterns. Presenting only the first proportion, as popular summaries often do, creates the impression of a near-universal rule while hiding a category that is common enough to matter clinically. Now add the dissociation logic that the classic cases supply. If damage to region A impairs task 1 but not task 2, while damage to region B impairs task 2 but not task 1, the double dissociation supports the claim that the two tasks depend on partially separable machinery. But the inference has limits: a dissociation shows separability of processes, not that region A is sufficient for task 1, and a single case with a large lesion cannot distinguish the damaged area from the fibres passing through it. That is why the modern reviews emphasise lesion-symptom mapping with larger samples and, increasingly, network analyses: they convert a compelling anecdote into a graded, testable claim.
lessons.question: Why does a double dissociation between two language impairments support separability of processes more strongly than a single case showing one impairment?
lessons.answer: Because each task is impaired by different damage while the other task is relatively spared, showing that the two functions are not simply one process measured twice.
lessons.distractor: Because two cases rule out the possibility of compensation, which a single case cannot address.
lessons.correction: The gain from a double dissociation is symmetry: with one case, a deficit could reflect a single general process that both tasks share, but when task 1 survives damage that breaks task 2 and the reverse also occurs, the two tasks cannot be reducible to one process. Compensation is a separate issue and is not what the double dissociation resolves; likewise, neither design by itself establishes that the damaged region is sufficient for the function, which requires additional evidence such as stimulation or reversible disruption in intact tissue.

depth.definitions: Aphasia is an acquired language impairment after brain damage. A dissociation is a pattern in which damage affects one function and spares another; a double dissociation is the mirrored pattern across two patients or two lesion groups. Lateralisation means the relative degree to which a function depends on one hemisphere. The dual-stream account describes a dorsal pathway linking auditory representations to articulation and a ventral pathway linking sound to meaning. Lesion-symptom mapping is the statistical association of damage locations with deficits across samples; voxel-based methods relate damage at each voxel to performance, and diffusion imaging maps white matter tracts. Prosody is the intonation and rhythm of speech, for which right-hemisphere contributions are documented. Prerequisites: necessity and sufficiency reasoning from lesson 28, reverse inference cautions from lesson 29, and lesion inference limits from lesson 40.
depth.mechanism: The classical model connected a production centre, a comprehension centre and a connecting tract, and damage anywhere in the circuit was expected to produce a predictable syndrome. The evidence that changed this picture is anatomical and functional. Anatomically, the regions named in the classical model are defined by maps such as Brodmann's, while the lesions that produce the syndromes extend across several areas and commonly involve underlying white matter, so the correlation between syndrome and named area is loose. Functionally, activation studies show distributed responses across both hemispheres during language tasks, and stimulation mapping shows that interruption of specific sites or tracts during a task can disrupt different components, which is stronger evidence for the involvement of those sites than a lesion is. The dual-stream account organises these findings into two routes with different computational jobs. Dronkers and colleagues emphasise that the field's methods themselves have driven the reinterpretation: each new method, from post-mortem anatomy to voxel-based lesion-symptom mapping to network analysis, redefined what a language area was taken to be.
depth.secondExample: Contrast a classical syndrome with the same deficit produced by subcortical damage. In the classical case, a cortical lesion in the left inferior frontal region produces non-fluent speech with impaired repetition and relatively preserved comprehension; the syndrome is named after the region. In subcortical cases, damage to the thalamus or to white matter tracts can produce deficits that resemble cortical syndromes, and Gupta and Srivastava explicitly review subcortical and thalamic contributions. If two different sites produce the same behavioural picture, then the picture does not identify the site, and any clinical inference from syndrome to location is weaker than the textbook suggests. The same logic explains why modern work emphasises tracts and networks: a tract carries information between regions, so interrupting it removes a component of a distributed process rather than a stored faculty.
depth.mistake: The persistent error is pop-lateralisation: left brain is logic and language, right brain is creativity, and a person can be trained to use the other side. Diagnostic correction: hemisphere differences in language are real but graded, the hemispheres interact continuously through the corpus callosum, and the popular traits-and-training claims are not supported by the dissociative evidence, which concerns deficits after damage. A second error is treating the classical syndromes as natural kinds; they are useful clusters whose boundaries are blurry, and the same clinical label can accompany different lesions. A third is over-reading activation: a region that is active during a language task is not thereby necessary for it, and the reverse inference problem described in lesson 29 applies directly.
depth.application: Task: given a hypothetical case in which a person has fluent but empty speech and impaired comprehension after a superior temporal lesion, write four lines: which classical syndrome this resembles; which modern account explains the pattern more precisely and why; what additional imaging would strengthen the localisation claim; and what you would refuse to conclude from the case alone. Self-review rubric: a point for naming the syndrome correctly as a description rather than an explanation; a point for invoking the ventral stream or the network account; a point for naming a method that tests necessity such as stimulation mapping or tract imaging; a point deducted for concluding that the named area is the language centre, and a point deducted for any statement about the person's ability to recover or to be treated.
depth.summary: Language is left-lateralised in a graded, population-level sense, with right-hemisphere contributions in prosody and other aspects, and it is supported by distributed cortical and subcortical systems organised into dorsal and ventral processing routes. The classical syndromes remain useful descriptions of behavioural clusters, and the evidence value of any lesion case depends on its design: single cases suggest, dissociations constrain, and stimulation or tract interruption tests necessity. Transfer: when a claim says that a region 'is' a language function, ask which method established necessity and whether the finding held across lesions and individuals.

lessons.title: Executive function and the limits of grey-matter claims
lessons.explanation: Objective: define the components grouped under executive function, identify the circuits usually implicated, and evaluate claims that training, practice or expertise changes grey matter. Executive function is an umbrella term for control processes that guide behaviour when habit and immediate stimulus are not enough: holding information in mind and manipulating it, inhibiting a prepotent response, and switching between rules or tasks. Neuroscience Online's chapter on higher cortical functions treats this under the association and executive processing material, with a section on the anterior association area that includes the prefrontal cortex and the classic case of frontal injury, and neighbouring sections on posterior association cortex and on contralateral neglect after right parietal damage. Two structural points matter for the claims that follow. First, association cortex is defined by its connectivity and its position between sensory and motor systems, which is why executive deficits after frontal damage are typically about how behaviour is organised rather than about a lost sensory or motor capacity. Second, executive measures are task measures: a Stroop task, a span task and a switching task each load on control processes differently, so 'improved executive function' is not a single quantity. The grey-matter half of the title concerns measurement. Structural differences are usually estimated from T1-weighted images by segmenting tissue classes and either counting voxel-wise tissue probability or measuring thickness and volume; these measures are indirect, and they respond to hydration, scanner and sequence differences, head motion, and analysis choices including smoothing and threshold. A change in a grey-matter measure is evidence that something about that tissue differed, not that neurons were added. The training literature then asks whether practice produces such changes and whether they matter: the systematic review by van Balkom and colleagues of controlled cognitive training trials with functional imaging found heterogeneity, with both increases and decreases in task-related activation reported and few studies demonstrating that neural change tracked cognitive change, while the meta-analysis by Melby-Lervag, Redick and Hulme found reliable immediate gains on intermediate-transfer measures and no convincing evidence for far transfer across ability, decoding, comprehension and arithmetic measures.
lessons.example: Do the sample-size arithmetic that most media summaries omit. For a two-group comparison at a two-tailed alpha of 0.05 with 80 per cent power, the approximate number per group is twice the square of 2.802 divided by the square of the effect size. For a small effect of 0.3 this gives 175 participants per group; for a moderate 0.5 it gives 63; for a large 0.9 it gives 20; for 1.2 it gives 11. A typical training study with 20 participants per group is therefore powered for a large effect and badly underpowered for a small one, so a null result from it is weak evidence of no effect and a positive result is inflated by the selection of studies that happened to produce large estimates. Put concrete units on it: if two groups differ by 2.5 per cent in a grey-matter volume whose between-subject standard deviation is 5 per cent, the standardised difference is 0.5, and detecting it needs about 63 people per group. Now the imaging version of the problem. If a whole-brain analysis tests 100,000 voxels at an uncorrected threshold of 0.001, about 100 voxels are expected to exceed threshold by chance alone; reporting those voxels as findings without correction is equivalent to reporting chance. A small number of comparisons needs care too: with three uncorrected tests at 0.05 the chance of at least one false positive is about 14 per cent, and with 14 tests it is about 51 per cent.
lessons.question: A study reports that eight weeks of training increased grey-matter volume in a frontal region, measured with voxel-based morphometry, and concludes that training grew new neurons. What is wrong with the conclusion?
lessons.answer: The measure estimates tissue properties from segmented images and cannot distinguish new neurons from changes in dendrites, glia, vasculature, water content or measurement variance.
lessons.distractor: Nothing is wrong, provided the increase survived whole-brain correction, because a corrected structural difference demonstrates tissue growth.
lessons.correction: Correction for multiple comparisons limits false positives; it does not make voxel-based morphometry a cell-counting method. A corrected difference is evidence that the segmented tissue probability differed, and the cellular interpretation requires other methods. The further step from 'something changed in a structure' to 'new neurons grew' is unsupported by the design, and the same study usually cannot say whether the change would persist after training stopped.

depth.definitions: Executive function is an umbrella label for control processes such as working memory updating, response inhibition and set shifting. The prefrontal cortex is the large anterior region including dorsolateral, ventrolateral, medial and orbital subdivisions with distinct connections. Voxel-based morphometry is a whole-brain method that compares local tissue probability or concentration across aligned images. Cortical thickness is estimated from the distance between the grey-white boundary and the pial surface. Near transfer is improvement on a task resembling the trained task; far transfer is improvement on distantly related abilities or everyday performance. Association cortex refers to areas receiving multimodal input and sending to other association and motor areas. Prerequisites: the imaging-inference material from lessons 27 and 40, together with the causal-inference cautions about reverse inference developed earlier in the course.
depth.mechanism: How control is implemented is described at two levels in these sources. At the systems level, association areas form long-range loops with each other and with subcortical structures, which is why frontal damage can produce disorganised behaviour while basic sensation and movement remain intact; Neuroscience Online illustrates this with the interconnectivity of association areas and with the behavioural consequences of prefrontal damage. At the cognitive level, models divide control into updating, inhibition and shifting, and each maps imperfectly onto anatomy, with substantial overlap in the frontoparietal networks engaged by different tasks. That imperfect mapping is why the effects of training are hard to interpret. If a task engages several networks, an activation change after training can reflect increased efficiency or increased effort, and the van Balkom review explicitly proposes both readings when it observes increases and decreases in the same literature; it also notes how few studies connect the neural change to the behavioural change. For structural measures there is an additional interpretive layer: voxel-based morphometry cannot separate cell types or their processes, so the honest statement is about tissue estimates, not about neurons.
depth.secondExample: Contrast a training study with an expertise study, both of which report structural differences. In a training study, participants are measured before and after an intervention, so time and measurement are held constant and the comparison is within person, but the sample is typically small and the measure is noisy, so the effect estimate is unstable. In an expertise study, trained and untrained groups are compared after the fact; here the same measurement is taken once in each group, but people selected themselves into the expertise, so differences may reflect who chose the activity, and the later longitudinal taxi driver work discussed in lesson 50 exists precisely because this design cannot separate selection from change. The lesson's arithmetic applies to both: an effect of 0.3 requires roughly 175 per group, and most studies reporting either design use far fewer, which is why the two designs disagree in the literature without either being obviously correct.
depth.mistake: The most common error is confusing a measure with a mechanism, as when a grey-matter difference is described as neurons, synapses or 'brain growth'. Diagnostic correction: name the measured quantity and then name the additional evidence that would be needed for the cellular claim. A second error is believing that a larger sample of trivia or 'brain games' transfers broadly; the meta-analytic evidence supports gains on closely related measures and does not support convincing far transfer, so claims about improved intelligence or everyday performance are not established. A third error is reversing the direction of causality in cross-sectional expertise studies. A fourth is presenting a single structural finding as a diagnostic or medical statement, which this educational material does not support.
depth.application: Task: choose one published claim that a cognitive intervention changed brain structure or activity, and write a 150-word audit with these four elements: the measured quantity stated in measurement terms; the design and its main alternative explanation; the sample size and the smallest effect it could detect at 80 per cent power; and one sentence on whether the neural change was shown to track the behavioural change. Self-review rubric: a point for stating the measure without mechanism language; a point for naming the specific alternative explanation; a point for an explicit power statement; a point for addressing the brain-behaviour linkage; deduct a point for any claim that a product improves general cognition.
depth.summary: Executive function is a set of control processes supported by distributed association networks, and the structural claims built on top of it rest on indirect image-derived measures. Power arithmetic and multiple-comparison arithmetic explain why small training studies produce unstable results, and the best meta-analytic evidence supports near and intermediate transfer while leaving far transfer unestablished. Transfer: convert any 'brain change' claim into a measurement claim plus the additional evidence required for the mechanism claim.
